subject: chemistry

moments.title: Arrhenius's dissertation
moments.body:
Arrhenius's PhD thesis proposes that salts dissociate into ions in water. The examiners are bewildered and award the lowest passing grade. He nearly fails.

Within 20 years the theory wins the 1903 Nobel.
moments.takeaway: A PhD thesis that nearly fails wins a Nobel Prize 19 years later.

moments.title: Arrhenius equation
moments.body: Arrhenius derives k = A exp(-Ea/RT). The exponential dependence of rate on temperature explains why 'a 10°C rise roughly doubles reaction rate'.
moments.takeaway: An exponential law links temperature to chemical rate.

moments.title: Transition state theory
moments.body: Eyring's transition state theory derives the Arrhenius pre-factor from statistical mechanics. Rate = (kT/h) exp(-Delta G‡/RT). The activation energy gets a structural interpretation.
moments.takeaway: Reaction rates become a problem in molecular geometry.

moments.title: Arrhenius and climate
moments.body: Arrhenius is also the first to calculate that doubling atmospheric CO2 would warm Earth by 5-6 °C (his estimate). He sees it as beneficial for Scandinavian agriculture.
moments.takeaway: The same chemist who explains kinetics also founds climate science.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Arrhenius plots (ln k vs 1/T) are standard for measuring activation energies. They underpin food preservation, drug stability, and modelling enzyme kinetics.
now.open_questions: Can computational chemistry predict activation energies to chemical accuracy (1 kcal/mol)?

reflection: Arrhenius's PhD examiners gave him a near-failing grade. The work won a Nobel Prize. How do you tell brilliance from nonsense when an idea is brand new?
